title: Preface
summary: NVIDIA Corporation’s Form 10-K cover identifies its fiscal year ended January 25, 2026, corporate and securities details, filing status, filer classification, internal-control attestation, shell-company status, market value and shares outstanding, and proxy materials incorporated by reference. The contents list Parts I–IV: business, risks, cybersecurity, properties, legal matters, equity and market information, management discussion, market risk, financial statements, controls and other disclosures; governance, executive compensation, ownership and related-party matters; exhibits, schedules, and a 10-K summary.

title: Where You Can Find More Information
summary: NVIDIA discloses material information through its investor relations website, press releases, SEC filings, public calls and webcasts, and listed social media channels, including its blogs, LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram, X, Threads, and YouTube. These channels may carry material information and support Regulation FD compliance, so investors should monitor them alongside traditional disclosures. The list may change, and channel content is not part of the Form 10-K.

title: Forward-Looking Statements
summary: The report explains that forward-looking statements are protected by securities-law safe harbors, based on management’s current beliefs, assumptions, and available information, and may be identified by common predictive terms. They are subject to risks and uncertainties that could make actual outcomes materially different; readers should consult the Risk Factors section and not rely unduly on them. Statements reflect only the filing date, and NVIDIA generally has no duty to update them. “NVIDIA,” “we,” “us,” “our,” and “Company” refer to NVIDIA Corporation and its subsidiaries. “We believe” statements likewise reflect filing-date opinions based on potentially limited information, not exhaustive review, and are inherently uncertain.

title: Item 1. Business Our Company

nodes.title: Item 1. Business Our Company (intro)
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its accelerated-computing and AI platform, combining GPUs, CUDA, software, networking, systems, models, data, and services across industries. It explains GPU-enabled AI applications, platform strategy, developer ecosystem, and major innovations from the GPU and CUDA through Blackwell Ultra and open AI models. Customers include cloud providers, enterprises, researchers, gamers, and creators; applications span AI, science, gaming, design, healthcare, finance, and transportation. The text gives company history, its Compute & Networking and Graphics segments, four target markets, and details Data Center products, networking, deployment, customers, and NVLink Fusion.

nodes.title: NVIDIA’s Businesses, Markets, and Customers
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its customers and uses across cloud AI, enterprise and startup applications, research and supercomputing, gaming, and professional creative and engineering work, including growing generative and agentic AI opportunities. It notes its founding and incorporation history. Its two reporting segments are Compute & Networking, covering data center, AI, networking, automotive, and related software, and Graphics, covering GeForce and Quadro/NVIDIA RTX GPUs. Its platforms combine processors, interconnects, software, algorithms, systems, and services and target four markets: Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive.

nodes.title: Data Center
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its Data Center business as a full-stack accelerated-computing platform for AI, HPC, graphics, robotics, and other workloads across cloud, enterprise, and edge settings. It combines GPUs, CPUs, networking, systems, software, services, libraries, models, and paid enterprise software, serving cloud providers, businesses, public-sector organizations, and industry partners. The text highlights NVLink Fusion, Blackwell and upcoming Rubin platforms, and physical-AI offerings. It also covers gaming products and RTX/DLSS innovations; professional visualization GPUs and software for design and content creation; and automotive’s DRIVE Hyperion end-to-end automated-driving platform.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Platforms and Market Segments
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its partner ecosystem, GPU-based accelerated computing and software platform, paid AI and virtual GPU software, Blackwell and Rubin systems, and end-to-end physical AI solutions. Gaming coverage includes market trends, GeForce products, RTX and DLSS technologies, and Blackwell RTX 50 Series and GeForce NOW launches. Professional Visualization covers GPU-accelerated design and content creation, ISV partnerships, and RTX PRO GPUs for AI-enabled workflows. The text also begins describing automotive automated-driving solutions through DRIVE Hyperion.

nodes.title: Automotive
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes partnerships across industries and its full-stack accelerated-computing platform: GPUs and co-designed data-center systems, extensive software, paid AI Enterprise and vGPU licenses, Blackwell and planned Rubin platforms, and physical-AI solutions. It outlines gaming products and technologies, including GeForce RTX, GeForce NOW, ray tracing, DLSS, and Blackwell RTX 50 GPUs; professional visualization services and RTX PRO GPUs for design and AI workflows; and the DRIVE Hyperion end-to-end automotive platform for autonomous driving and in-vehicle services.

nodes.title: Business Strategies
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s strategy centers on advancing its unified accelerated-computing platform across data centers, gaming, visualization, and automotive; extending AI leadership through end-to-end hardware, software, products, and a broad developer and partner ecosystem; advancing AI-enabled graphics, RTX, and Omniverse; developing DRIVE autonomous-vehicle solutions; and licensing or custom-developing its IP. The text also covers worldwide partner-led sales and technical support, developer engagement and training, gaming seasonality, fabless manufacturing and supplier diversification, and intense competition driven by technology, performance, software, distribution, manufacturing, and cost factors.

nodes.title: Sales, Seasonality, and Manufacturing
nodes.summary: The page describes licensing and development arrangements that extend the reach of the company’s IP; global sales and marketing, partner relationships, technical and pre-sales support, and developer programs and training. It notes that desktop gaming revenue is typically stronger in the fiscal year’s second half, though trends may not repeat. It outlines a fabless manufacturing model using certified suppliers, advance supply commitments during growth, efforts to diversify supply geographically, and key wafer, memory, packaging, assembly, testing, and packaging partners.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: The market is intensely competitive, with rapid technological change and evolving standards. Success depends on performance, product range, customer and partner access, distribution, software support, API compliance, manufacturing, pricing, system costs, anticipating demand, and delivering quality products reliably at competitive prices. Competition is expected to grow, including from lower-priced or higher-performing offerings, new entrants, and alliances; some rivals have greater resources or adaptability. Competitors span GPU, CPU, DPU, SoC, AI and accelerated-computing hardware and software, cloud companies’ internally designed platforms, Arm CPU suppliers, SoC providers for servers and embedded devices, and networking and interconnect suppliers. Named competitors include AMD, Huawei, Intel, Alibaba, Alphabet, Amazon, Baidu, Microsoft, Ambarella, Broadcom, Qualcomm, Renesas, Samsung, Tesla, Arista, Cisco, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Lumentum, and Marvell, plus internal design teams at cloud and systems companies.

nodes.title: Patents and Proprietary Rights
nodes.summary: The company protects its U.S. and international intellectual property through patents, trademarks, trade secrets, nondisclosure agreements, licenses, and foreign laws and treaties. Its issued patents expire from March 2026 to June 2045, with additional patents issued, allowed, or pending, mainly covering its products and related technology. Some countries, including in Asia, offer weaker protection, increasing piracy risk. The company evaluates where to seek formal protection based on manufacturing locations, strategic priorities, enforcement of IP laws, and commercial significance, and expects to continue licensing third-party technology.

nodes.title: Government Regulations
nodes.summary: The text describes shifting U.S. export controls affecting the company’s chips, systems, software, and technology, especially sales to China, Russia, and other countries. It details licensing restrictions and changes for A100/H100, H20, and H200 products; related charges, limited licensed revenue, tariffs, inspection requirements, and sales risks. The company says it is effectively excluded from China’s data center market, aiding competitors, while licensing uncertainty and possible worldwide controls threaten support, demand, and long-term competitiveness. Chinese policies also risk Gaming and Data Center revenue, and Asia-focused supply chains may be disrupted. Other current compliance has not materially affected operations or capital spending, but a broad range of existing or future regulations could raise costs and harm results.

nodes.title: Human Capital Management
nodes.summary: At fiscal year-end 2026, the company had about 42,000 employees across 38 countries: 31,000 in R&D and 11,000 in other functions. Its talent strategy emphasizes recruiting, developing, and retaining global talent. Over 80% held technical roles, more than half had advanced degrees, over 40% of new hires came through referrals, and turnover was 3.7%. Development includes on-the-job training and tuition reimbursement; compensation and benefits reward performance and align interests through equity, health, and financial wellness programs. Employee listening supports an inclusive, merit-based culture.

nodes.title: Information About Our Executive Officers
nodes.summary: The text lists NVIDIA’s five executive officers, their ages and roles as of February 20, 2026, and summarizes their careers and education. CEO Jen-Hsun Huang co-founded NVIDIA and previously worked at LSI Logic and AMD. CFO Colette Kress joined in 2013 after finance roles at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments. Ajay Puri, head of Worldwide Field Operations since 2009, joined in 2005 after roles at Sun Microsystems and other technology and consulting firms. Operations leader Debora Shoquist joined in 2007 after executive roles at JDS Uniphase, Coherent, Quantum and Hewlett-Packard. General Counsel Timothy Teter joined in 2017 after more than two decades litigating technology and patent matters at Cooley and earlier engineering work at Lockheed. The text also gives each officer’s degrees.

nodes.title: Available Information
nodes.summary: NVIDIA provides its Forms 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, and applicable amendments free on its website as soon as reasonably practicable after filing or furnishing them to the SEC. The SEC website also provides electronically filed reports, proxy and information statements, and other issuer information. NVIDIA’s website and linked content are not part of this annual report.

summary: NVIDIA presents its accelerated-computing and AI platform, company history, business segments, four markets, products, technologies, customers, and applications across data centers, gaming, professional visualization, and automotive. It describes strategy, licensing, global sales and developer support, seasonality, fabless manufacturing and suppliers, and competition. The section also covers intellectual-property protections, export controls and other regulation, workforce and talent practices, executive officers and their backgrounds, and where investors can access SEC filings.

title: Item 1A. Risk Factors

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Industry and Markets
nodes.summary: The section notes that listed and currently unknown or immaterial risks could harm the company’s business, financial condition, results, reputation, or stock price. Industry and market risks include failing to meet evolving needs and competition, either of which could reduce financial results; competition may also diminish market share.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Demand, Supply, and Manufacturing
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from demand forecasting errors, long manufacturing lead times, supply and capacity uncertainty, third-party manufacturing dependence, and product defects. It also covers global business risks, including economic and international exposure, cybersecurity and data breaches, business disruptions, climate change, investment and acquisition outcomes, customer and partner concentration, counterparty risk, retaining key staff, disruptions to business processes and information systems, and fluctuating results that may disappoint investors and lower the stock price.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Regulatory, Legal, Our Stock, and Other Matters
nodes.summary: The text outlines regulatory, legal, stock, and other risks: complex laws and export restrictions; scrutiny of sustainability and responsible technology use, including AI; costly or inadequate intellectual-property protection; changing privacy and security obligations; tax liabilities and law changes; litigation, investigations, and regulatory proceedings; and Delaware law, governing documents, and the Microsoft agreement potentially delaying or preventing a change in control. These risks may harm operations, finances, reputation, competitiveness, or product sales.

nodes.title: Risk Factors
nodes.summary: The company warns that rapid technological, customer, competitive, and standards changes could harm results if it cannot adapt, develop and launch products and software or cloud offerings, expand its ecosystem, meet safety and compliance expectations, manage product lifecycles, scale infrastructure, and fund necessary investments. R&D in newer markets, uncertain adoption and revenue, lengthy design-win processes, and failure to deliver customer value pose risks. Groq’s costly, nonrefundable licensed technology may be difficult to integrate, delayed, unsuccessful, or unprofitable. Changing availability and timing of contracted cloud services may disrupt costs, revenue, and development. Standalone software offerings may incur significant costs without meaningful sales or returns.

nodes.title: Competition could adversely impact our market share and financial results.
nodes.summary: Intensifying competition could reduce market share, demand, selling prices, and financial results as offerings, standards, customer needs, entrants, and industry consolidation evolve. Competitors may offer cheaper or better products and have advantages in fabrication, experience, customers, IP, design wins, and financial and commercial resources, enabling faster innovation, expansion, and access to scarce manufacturing capacity and materials. Customers may replace the company’s solutions with in-house products; competing cloud AI services could also limit its scale. Failure to compete successfully could harm the business.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Demand, Supply, and Manufacturing Long manufacturing lead times and uncertain supply and capacity availability, combined with a failure to estimate customer demand accurately, has led and could lead to mismatches between supply and demand.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from long, uncertain manufacturing lead times, supply constraints, and inaccurate or volatile demand forecasts, which can cause shortages, excess inventory, lost sales, reputational damage, price reductions, penalties, write-downs, impairments, and lower margins. Demand is affected by market, technology, customer, channel, policy, economic, infrastructure, and geopolitical factors, including data-center capacity, energy, capital, and AI adoption. Growing commitments, prepayments, supplier complexity, domestic manufacturing scale-up, and frequent product and architecture transitions add risk; delays, quality issues, shifting customer adoption, and incompatible inventory may disrupt revenue. New or speculative uses such as cryptocurrency mining, changing standards, and gray-market resale further complicate forecasting. The company expects Gaming supply constraints from fiscal 2027’s first quarter onward.

nodes.title: Dependency on third-party suppliers and their technology to manufacture, assemble, test, or package our products reduces our control over product quantity and quality, manufacturing yields, and product delivery schedules and could harm our business.
nodes.summary: The company relies on third-party foundries and subcontractors to manufacture, assemble, test, and package products, limiting its control over supply, quality, yields, and delivery. Supplier-related risks include insufficient or withdrawn capacity, inaccurate demand forecasts and higher prices, raw-material or technology failures, regulatory noncompliance, concentrated suppliers, replacement and integration costs, unqualified product changes, competitors receiving priority, inflexible or prepaid orders, low yields, longer lead times, and disruption from natural disasters, power conservation, pandemics, or cyberattacks. These risks may prevent meeting demand or scaling supply and harm operations, margins, revenue, and financial results.

nodes.title: Defects in our products have caused and could cause us to incur significant expenses to remediate, which can damage our reputation and cause us to lose market share.
nodes.summary: Complex hardware, software, services, and AI products may contain defects, vulnerabilities, failures, poor performance, or bias—especially with new technologies, releases, third-party training data, or partner-supplied components—and issues may emerge only after shipment. These problems can expose data, damage integrated products and users, disrupt supply, and require costly repairs, replacements, recalls, inventory write-offs, customer reimbursements, indemnities, or regulatory fines. Remediation may be inadequate or late, divert staff, undermine customer relationships, market acceptance, design wins, brand, revenue, margins, and financial results. Product-liability defense costs can be substantial even when third parties are responsible, while insurance may be insufficient or unavailable.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Global Operating Business Adverse economic conditions may harm our business.
nodes.summary: Economic, industry, geopolitical, and policy uncertainty—including recession, inflation, tariffs, supply-chain constraints, and financial-market disruption—could raise costs, reduce margins and demand, disrupt suppliers, limit forecasting, increase insolvencies and credit risks, and impair customers’ ability to operate or pay. Bank instability may disrupt liquidity and contractual obligations. The company’s liquid investment portfolio, mostly U.S. government securities, faces credit, liquidity, market, and interest-rate risks; prolonged downturns or a U.S. credit downgrade could reduce investment values, trigger losses or impairment charges, and cause broader financial-market effects.

nodes.title: International sales and operations are a significant part of our business, which exposes us to risks that could harm our business.
nodes.summary: International sales and overseas operations, including third-party manufacturing, account for 31% of fiscal 2026 revenue and expose the company to material risks. These include intense competition in China, where exports are restricted; economic and political conditions; health-related lockdowns; differing IP, employment, legal, and business practices; capital-market disruption, anti-inflation measures, and currency fluctuations; natural disasters, war, terrorism, and other catastrophic events; and trade restrictions such as tariffs, sanctions, and import or export controls.

nodes.title: Product, system security, and data protection incidents or breaches, as well as cyber-attacks, could disrupt our operations, reduce our expected revenue, increase our expenses, and significantly harm our business and reputation.
nodes.summary: Cybersecurity incidents—from increasingly sophisticated malware, ransomware, AI-enabled, geopolitical, insider, and supply-chain attacks—could disrupt operations, reduce revenue, raise costs, and damage business, reputation, and stock price. Recovery may be constrained by compromised backups or limited access to suppliers’ systems. Risks include vulnerabilities in third-party systems and AI training data, exposure of sensitive information and partner source code, and impacts across customers. Prevention, monitoring, training, remediation, and compliance require ongoing investment but cannot eliminate threats or delays. Incidents or perceived breaches may trigger data loss, service and supply disruptions, liability, litigation, regulatory action, mandatory disclosures, reputational harm, and financial losses; public information gathering may also reveal competitively sensitive details.

nodes.title: Business disruptions could harm our operations, lead to a decline in revenue and increase our costs.
nodes.summary: Disasters, infrastructure failures, cyberattacks, supplier or third-party outages, political instability, conflict, regulatory changes, and other disruptions could interrupt operations, raise costs, reduce revenue, and materially harm results. Concentrated operations and suppliers in California and Asia create geographic risks; geopolitical tensions, including around Israel and regions involved in manufacturing, could affect markets, hiring, demand, and profitability. The company monitors the Israel conflict, which has caused limited disruption from employee military service but could have greater future effects. Business continuity plans may be inadequate. Growing reliance on cloud providers and data centers increases exposure to outages or insolvency, while water, energy, land, permitting, or regulatory constraints could limit customer data-center growth and demand.

nodes.title: Climate change may have a long-term impact on our business.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from climate change, including operational and supply-chain disruptions, extreme weather, insurance gaps, sustainability regulation and litigation, reputational concerns, unmet goals, and energy-use perceptions. It discusses risks and costs of acquisitions and strategic investments, including integration, regulatory, financing, impairment, and execution challenges; a proposed OpenAI partnership is not assured. It also describes revenue concentration and dependence on partners, distributors, and major customers; counterparty and potential financing risks in commercial arrangements; and challenges attracting, retaining, and succeeding executives and key employees.

nodes.title: Business, Customer, Counterparty, and Talent Risks
key_items: Commercial arrangements expose us to counterparty risks.
If we are unable to attract, retain and motivate our executives and key employees, our business may be harmed.
nodes.summary: The page outlines acquisition-integration challenges, including costs, delays, cybersecurity exposure, and possible harm to employee, vendor, and customer relationships. Revenue is concentrated among a few direct and indirect customers and partners; cancellations, changing purchasing patterns, trade restrictions, collection problems, or channel constraints could hurt results. Commercial commitments and potential customer financing create counterparty, credit, and cash-flow risks. Recruiting and retaining key talent may be hindered by competition, regulation, compensation costs, stock volatility, and inadequate succession planning.

nodes.title: Systems, Internal Controls, and Operating Results Risks
key_items: Our business is dependent upon the proper functioning of our business processes and information systems and modification or interruption of such systems may disrupt our business and internal controls.

Our operating results have in the past fluctuated and may in the future fluctuate, and if our operating results are below the expectations of securities analysts or investors, our stock price could decline.
nodes.summary: The company depends on reliable business processes and information systems, including ERP implementation and controls required by Sarbanes-Oxley; disruptions or implementation problems could impair operations, reporting, and controls. Material weaknesses may prompt investor concern, costs, restatements, delayed reporting, restricted capital-market access, stock declines, or regulatory action. Results may fluctuate due to spending flexibility, customer contracts and payment risks, vendor terms, environmental costs, and accounting changes. Cash-flow pressures and mismatched expense and revenue growth may undermine profitability; missing expectations could lower or destabilize the stock price.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Regulatory, Legal, Our Stock and Other Matters We are subject to complex laws, rules, regulations, and political and other actions, including restrictions on the export of our products, which may adversely impact our business.
nodes.summary: The text describes how complex and changing global laws, regulatory scrutiny, AI rules, sanctions, and trade policies can raise costs, constrain operations, damage relationships and reputation, and harm NVIDIA’s business and financial results. It details competition inquiries and AI regulation; export controls, tariffs, licensing, and geopolitical restrictions affecting products, customers, supply chains, and services; U.S. controls and China-related developments, including H20 losses, limited H200 licensing, and effective exclusion from China’s data-center market; potential worldwide controls, chip mandates, and restrictions on gaming, networking, automotive, and open-source AI products; competitive and demand effects, compliance risks, and reliance on Taiwanese and South Korean suppliers.

nodes.title: Scrutiny from shareholders, regulators and others regarding our corporate sustainability practices could result in additional costs or risks and adversely impact our reputation and willingness of customers and suppliers to do business with us.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from sustainability scrutiny, evolving stakeholder expectations, differing regulations, compliance costs, business restrictions, and reputational harm. It also covers risks from responsible AI use, including ethical and social concerns, legal liability, regulation, increased costs, operational changes, and slower adoption. Finally, it outlines intellectual-property litigation and enforcement costs, potential damages, licensing or sales restrictions, indemnification exposure, limits of protections across countries, theft or misuse of trade secrets, employee departures, and uncertainty over obtaining enforceable IP rights.

nodes.title: Sustainability, AI, and Intellectual Property Risks
key_items: Issues relating to the responsible use of our technologies, including AI in our offerings, may result in reputational or financial harm and liability.

Actions to adequately protect our IP rights could result in substantial costs to us and our ability to compete could be harmed if we are unsuccessful or if we are prohibited from making or selling our products.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from sustainability practices, oversight, disclosure, and compliance that may increase costs, restrict business relationships, or harm reputation and expose the company to liability. It covers legal, ethical, social, regulatory, operational, and reputational risks from using AI, including increased compliance costs and possible limits on products and adoption. It also outlines IP litigation, enforcement and licensing costs, potential damages or product restrictions, and the risk that inadequate protection, foreign-law limitations, theft, or unenforceable rights could weaken competitiveness and reduce returns on innovation.

nodes.title: We are subject to stringent and changing data privacy and security laws, rules, regulations and other obligations. These areas could damage our reputation, deter current and potential customers, affect our product design, or result in legal or regulatory proceedings and liability.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from extensive, changing privacy and security obligations worldwide, including U.S. state and federal laws, GDPR/U.K. GDPR, AI rules, NIS2, and data localization and cross-border transfer restrictions in Europe, China, and elsewhere. Noncompliance, breaches, or misleading privacy claims could trigger fines, litigation, operational changes, transfer limits, reputational harm, and material business or financial impacts. It also warns that tax audits, legal changes, U.S. rates and FDDEI, OECD Pillar One/Two rules, and other factors may raise taxes and hurt results. Finally, ongoing litigation and investigations—including a securities class action over 2017–18 channel inventory and cryptocurrency-related GPU demand—could be costly, disruptive, or produce damages, injunctions, or other adverse outcomes.

nodes.title: Privacy, Tax, and Legal Risks
key_items: We may have exposure to additional tax liabilities and our operating results may be adversely impacted by changes in tax laws, higher than expected tax rates and other tax-related factors.
Our business is exposed to the burden and risks associated with litigation, investigations and regulatory proceedings.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from privacy and security obligations, breaches, changing data-protection laws, and potentially misleading disclosures, which may lead to enforcement, litigation, fines, processing restrictions, and reputational or financial harm. It also outlines tax audit exposure, changing U.S. and international tax rules—including FDDEI and OECD Pillar One and Two—plus other factors that may raise tax rates, costs, and liabilities. Finally, it discusses ongoing and future litigation, investigations, and regulatory proceedings, their uncertainty and potential remedies, and their costs and operational disruption.

nodes.title: Delaware law and our certificate of incorporation, bylaws and agreement with Microsoft could delay or prevent a change in control.
nodes.summary: Delaware anti-takeover law, NVIDIA’s charter and bylaws, and its Microsoft Xbox agreement may delay or prevent a change in control. The charter and bylaws let the board issue preferred stock, change its size, and amend bylaws without shareholder approval; prohibit written shareholder consent; impose advance notice rules for nominations and proposals; and require supermajority votes to amend certain provisions. If an offer targets at least 30% of common stock, Microsoft may have first and last rights of refusal. These restrictions may discourage proxy contests and limit shareholders’ ability to elect directors or pursue desired corporate actions.

summary: The section warns that known and emerging risks could harm NVIDIA’s business, finances, reputation, or stock price. It covers rapid technological and market change, competition, uncertain demand, long manufacturing lead times, supplier dependence, capacity and product-quality risks, and challenges developing new products, AI and software offerings, scaling infrastructure, and integrating Groq technology. It also addresses economic and international exposure; cyber, data, operational, climate, acquisition, customer, counterparty, talent, systems, internal-control, and earnings risks; and complex regulation, export controls, sustainability and AI scrutiny, privacy, intellectual property, taxes, litigation, and proceedings. Delaware law, corporate documents, and the Microsoft agreement may constrain shareholder actions or delay a change in control.

title: Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments
key_items: Item 1C. Cybersecurity Risk management and strategy; Governance
Item 1C. Cybersecurity Risk management and strategy
summary: The filing reports no unresolved staff comments. It describes cybersecurity risk management aligned generally with ISO 27001, including evolving safeguards, external expert advice, integrated risk processes, privacy and security training and policies, and risk-based vendor reviews and standards assessments; it refers readers to Item 1A for related risks. Governance rests with the Board and Audit Committee, which receive regular and annual security updates. Executive cross-functional teams review threats and guide practices and incident response. A Chief Security Officer with over 18 years of government and private-sector experience oversees material cybersecurity risks.

title: Properties, Legal Proceedings, and Mine Safety
summary: The company is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, and owns and leases about 3 million square feet of office and building space, along with data centers and other facilities in the U.S. and several international locations. It considers its facilities suitable and does not allocate assets by operating segment; lease obligations are discussed in a referenced financial-statement note. Legal proceedings are covered in another referenced note. Mine safety disclosures are not applicable. The page then begins Part II.

title: Item 7. Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
key_items: Overview; Our Company and Our Businesses
Recent Developments, Future Objectives and Challenges
summary: NVIDIA’s MD&A overview describes its evolution into an AI infrastructure company, its Compute & Networking and Graphics segments, and its corporate history. Fiscal 2026 growth was led by Data Center AI, with Blackwell dominating; it discusses product launches and transition risks, infrastructure and energy constraints, China export licensing and H20 charges, open-source AI competition, supply-chain expansion, investments and guarantees, and macroeconomic pressures. Results include revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65%, segment growth, lower gross margin, and higher operating expenses.

title: Critical Accounting Estimates
key_items: Inventories; Income Taxes; Non-Marketable Equity Securities
Revenue Recognition Revenue Allowances; Contracts with Multiple Performance Obligations
summary: The text outlines critical accounting estimates under U.S. GAAP for inventory, income taxes, private-company equity securities, and revenue recognition. Inventory write-downs and purchase commitments rely on demand, market, lead-time, and other judgments; they reduced gross margin by 2.6% in fiscal 2026 and 2.3% in 2025. Tax estimates cover deferred taxes, contingencies, valuation allowances, uncertain positions, interest, and penalties. Private equity investments use the measurement alternative and quarterly impairment reviews. Revenue estimates include returns, rebates, and marketing funds; multi-obligation contracts require judgment about distinct obligations and allocation of transaction price using standalone selling prices.

title: Results of Operations

nodes.title: Results of Operations (intro)
nodes.summary: The section introduces a comparison of fiscal 2026 and 2025 financial condition and operating results, directing readers to the 2025-versus-2024 discussion in NVIDIA’s prior Form 10-K. It presents income-statement items as percentages of revenue, including revenue, costs, profits, operating expenses, income, and taxes, and reports segment revenue for Compute & Networking and Graphics.

nodes.title: Operating Income by Reportable Segments
key_items: Compute & Networking revenue; Reportable segment operating income
nodes.summary: For the year ended Jan. 25, 2026, Compute & Networking revenue was $193.5 billion and Graphics revenue $22.5 billion, totaling $215.9 billion; segment operating income was $130.1 billion and $9.2 billion, totaling $139.3 billion. Year-over-year revenue growth reflected accelerated computing and AI: Data Center computing rose 59% on Blackwell demand, networking 142% with NVLink, Ethernet, and InfiniBand growth, and Graphics grew on Blackwell sales. Operating income increased in both segments; Compute & Networking growth was partly offset by a $4.5 billion H20 inventory and purchase-obligation charge in Q1 FY2026. The text also presents prior-year comparisons, dollar and percentage changes, and financial ratios.

nodes.title: Revenue Concentration and Gross Margins
nodes.summary: Defines direct and indirect customers and notes revenue concentration among a limited number of them. Reports major direct-customer revenue shares for fiscal years 2024–2026, indirect-customer estimation methods and significant contributions—including cloud services attributed to an AI research and deployment company—and geographic revenue based on customer headquarters. Defines gross profit and its cost components, then explains fiscal 2026 margin decline amid the shift to Blackwell datacenter solutions and a $4.5 billion H20 charge. Details inventory-related provisions, releases, and their unfavorable gross-margin effects for fiscal 2025 and 2026.

nodes.title: Operating Expenses
nodes.summary: Fiscal 2026 operating expenses rose to $23.1 billion from $16.4 billion: R&D increased 43%, driven by compensation and benefits (up 29%) and compute/infrastructure (up 79%); sales, general and administrative expenses increased mainly due to compensation and benefits. Total other income was $11.1 billion versus $8.5 billion in 2025, reflecting higher interest income from increased cash and securities and investment gains, including Intel shares; interest expense mainly comprises note coupons and debt-discount amortization. Income tax expense was $21.4 billion versus $11.1 billion, with effective rates of 15.1% and 13.3%; the rate increase reflected relatively lower stock-compensation, FDDEI, and research-credit benefits. Rates remained below the 21% federal statutory rate due to these and other tax benefits. The company recognized currently effective OBBBA provisions and released $711 million of state deferred-tax valuation allowance. Cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities totaled $62.6 billion at January 25, 2026, versus $43.2 billion a year earlier.

nodes.title: Other Income and Income Taxes
nodes.summary: The page notes fiscal 2026 sales, general, and administrative expense growth was driven mainly by compensation and benefits. It reports other income components and year-over-year changes, explaining higher interest income from increased cash and investments, interest expense from notes, and investment and currency-related gains, including Intel stock gains. It compares fiscal 2026 and 2025 income tax expense and effective rates, explains rate changes and tax benefits, describes enacted OBBBA provisions, and reports release of a $711 million state deferred-tax valuation allowance. nodes.title: Note 1 - Organization and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
Organization and Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s accounting policies describe its incorporation, headquarters, terminology, and a reclassification of prior-year balances. Fiscal years end on the last Sunday in January and may span 52 or 53 weeks. Consolidated statements include wholly owned subsidiaries, with intercompany items eliminated. U.S. GAAP estimates affect reported amounts and are regularly reviewed, though actual results may differ. Revenue follows the five-step contract and performance-obligation process. Product revenue is recognized on transfer of control; support and warranties over service periods; returns, rebates, partner marketing funds, and customer taxes are treated as described in the revenue policies.

key_items: Foreign Currency Derivatives; Facility Lease Guarantees
NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary: NVIDIA uses foreign currency forwards to hedge operating expenses and monetary assets and liabilities. Expense hedges are designated, highly effective, and their gains or losses flow through accumulated other comprehensive income before reclassification to operating expense; effects were insignificant in fiscal 2026 and 2025. Non-designated contracts’ fair-value changes in other income or expense offset changes on hedged items. Fair values, expected near-term realized amounts, and deferred gains or losses were insignificant; contracts mature within 18 months. In 2026, NVIDIA also guaranteed partners’ facility leases in exchange for warrants, with maximum exposure of $3.5 billion over 5–7 years, reduced by partner payments and mitigated by $712 million in escrow. key_items: Revenue by End Market:; Long-lived assets:
nodes.summary: The text presents NVIDIA’s revenue by end market—Data Center, Compute Networking, Gaming, Professional Visualization, Automotive, OEM and Other, and total revenue—for three fiscal years, in millions. It also summarizes long-lived assets by country (United States, Taiwan, Israel, Other, and total) for January 25, 2026 and January 26, 2025, noting that these assets include property and equipment but exclude other assets, operating lease assets, goodwill, and intangible assets.

The note explains NVIDIA’s two reportable segments, the CEO’s role as CODM, how segment costs are allocated, and reporting policies, including consolidated expense review, no intersegment transactions, and no review of segment assets. It presents fiscal 2024–2026 segment revenue, operating income, other items, depreciation and amortization, and reconciliations to consolidated pretax income; revenue by end market and geography, including a 2026 methodology change, Taiwan attribution estimate, overseas shares, and U.S. demand trends; significant direct-customer revenue concentrations and customer definitions; and long-lived assets by country for 2025 and 2026, with asset exclusions specified.

nodes.title: Note 17 - Leases
nodes.summary: The company’s lease obligations are primarily operating leases for offices and data centers, expiring between fiscal years 2027 and 2041. As of January 25, 2026, future minimum payments total $3.624 billion; after $680 million of imputed interest, their present value is $2.944 billion, comprising $372 million of short-term and $2.572 billion of long-term liabilities. From fiscal 2027 through 2030, the company expects to begin leases with $22.7 billion in future obligations, primarily for data centers supporting research and development, with terms of 1.8 to 20 years.

summary: The notes cover accounting policies, upcoming disclosure rules, and the Groq technology license; stock-based compensation and earnings per share; goodwill, intangible assets, cash, securities, and investments; balance-sheet accounts, derivatives, debt, leases, commitments, warranties, and litigation; and income taxes, tax benefits, shareholder returns, and retirement plans. They also detail segment reporting, revenue by market and geography, customer concentration, and long-lived assets, with related valuations, rollforwards, maturities, and expected future payments or recognition.

title: NVIDIA Operating Lease Costs and Cash Flows
key_items: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
summary: NVIDIA reports operating lease costs of $462 million, $356 million, and $269 million for fiscal 2026, 2025, and 2024; short-term and variable lease costs were not significant. Supplemental information lists operating lease cash flows and lease assets obtained in exchange for obligations for the years ended January 25, 2026, January 26, 2025, and January 28, 2024. At January 25, 2026, leases had an 8.8-year weighted-average remaining term and 4.38% discount rate, versus 6.5 years and 4.16% at January 26, 2025.

title: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Schedule II – Valuation and Qualifying Accounts
key_items: Fiscal year 2026; Fiscal year 2025; Fiscal year 2024
summary: NVIDIA’s Schedule II reports beginning balances, additions, deductions, and ending balances for doubtful-account allowances, sales-return allowances, and deferred-tax valuation allowances for fiscal years 2024–2026, in millions. Notes explain that additions and deductions reflect expenses or acquired balances and write-offs; sales-return additions are estimated returns charged against revenue, with deductions representing returns; and deferred-tax additions reflect increased allowances on certain state and other tax assets, while deductions mainly reflect releases. Further details are referenced in Note 13.

nodes.title: Title
nodes.summary: The text lists company officers and directors, all dated February 25, 2026, then presents NVIDIA’s global Insider Trading Policy. It applies to employees, directors, contractors, consultants, and their trading agents, and warns about household members’ trades. It defines material non-public information (MNPI) and gives examples; prohibits trading while possessing MNPI, tipping, and certain NVIDIA derivatives, hedging, shorting, margin purchases, pledging, and unauthorized disclosures. Designated Individuals face quarterly trading and gifting blackout periods, with an exception for qualifying 10b5-1 plans. Policy ownership, scope, and dates are stated.

nodes.title: Insider Trading Policy and Trading Restrictions
key_items: ADDITIONAL RESTRICTIONS APPLICABLE TO “DESIGNATED INDIVIDUALS” ONLY
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s global policy applies to employees, directors, contractors, consultants, and trades made on their behalf; household and influenced persons’ trading can create legal risk. It defines material non-public information (MNPI), gives examples, and assigns responsibility for compliance. Laws prohibit trading while possessing relevant MNPI and tipping others. Regardless of MNPI or trading windows, NVIDIA derivatives, hedging, shorting, margin purchases or holdings, pledging securities, and unauthorized disclosures to the press or financial community are prohibited. Designated Individuals must check their status and may not trade or gift NVIDIA securities during quarterly closed windows, except under a 10b5-1 plan. The page also identifies the policy owner, dates, and page number.

nodes.title: Insider Trading Restrictions, Exceptions, and Reporting
nodes.summary: NVIDIA may impose temporary special trading restrictions on anyone exposed to risky nonpublic information. The policy lists exceptions for existing 10b5-1 plans, RSU tax withholding, ESPP participation, approved diversified exchange funds, eligible mutual funds and products, and qualifying gifts. Section 16 directors and officers need advance preclearance. Violations can bring legal penalties and employment discipline. Report concerns to Corporate Legal or anonymously through Speak Up; good-faith reporters are protected from retaliation. Direct questions to Corporate Legal before trading or sharing potential MNPI.

nodes.title: EXHIBIT 21.1
nodes.summary: Exhibit 21.1 lists NVIDIA Corporation subsidiaries as of January 25, 2026, excluding subsidiaries that are not significant in aggregate. It identifies three wholly owned subsidiaries and their jurisdictions: Mellanox Technologies, Ltd. (Israel), NVIDIA International, Inc. (Delaware, U.S.), and NVIDIA Singapore Pte Ltd (Singapore).

title: I, Jen-Hsun Huang, certify that:
summary: Exhibits 31.1 and 31.2 contain matching Sarbanes-Oxley certifications by NVIDIA CEO Jen-Hsun Huang and CFO Colette M. Kress, dated February 25, 2026. They attest to reviewing the 10-K, its lack of material misstatements or omissions, fair presentation of financial information, responsibility for designing and evaluating disclosure and financial-reporting controls, disclosure of material control changes and weaknesses, and reporting relevant fraud to auditors and the audit committee. Exhibits 32.1 and 32.2 certify under Exchange Act Rule 13a-14(b) and Section 906 that the 10-K for the year ended January 25, 2026 complies with applicable reporting requirements and fairly presents financial condition and results. Signed originals are retained by NVIDIA for possible SEC production; these certifications accompany but are not deemed filed or incorporated by reference.
